Case

  • A 24-year-old male presented with left flank pain for 2 days.
  • Next?
Notes

R O A D M A P

Notes

The Case at a Glance

The whole lecture follows one patient through three stages. Learn the stages and you have the skeleton of renal colic management.

STAGE 1 · PRESENTATION Uncomplicated colic 24-year-old male, left flank pain for 2 days: sudden, 10/10, radiating to the groin. Afebrile, no urinary or GI symptoms, left flank tenderness. Do: hydration · analgesia · medical expulsive therapy→STAGE 2 · DETERIORATION Obstructed + infected kidney Returns with fever and worse pain. WBC ↑, renal profile normal, CT shows the same stone. Do: cultures → broad-spectrum antibiotics → urgent urine diversion (DJ stent)→STAGE 3 · RECOVERY Infection cleared DJ stent inserted; 2 weeks later urine culture is negative. Do: definitive stone treatment (ESWL / URS / PCNL) chosen by site and size
THE ONE-LINE SUMMARY
Uncomplicated colic → conservative. Obstruction + infection → drain first, antibiotics alongside. Infection gone → remove the stone.

H I S T O R Y & E X A M I N A T I O N

  • 25-year-old woman, left flank pain, CT: 6 mm left ureteric stone, no complication → conservative (analgesia, hydration, MET). 438

History

  • Pain
  • Urinary symptoms
  • Eliminate differential diagnosis
Notes

Clinical Assessment

History — three jobs

1 Characterise the pain Onset (sudden?) and duration Severity (often 10/10) Radiation: loin → groin Aggravating / relieving factors, relation to movement·2 Urinary symptoms Haematuria Dysuria, frequency, urgency Their absence does not exclude a stone (as in this case)·3 Eliminate the differentials GI symptoms (vomiting, bowel change) Fever — infection changes everything Chest, gynae and testicular symptoms

Physical Examination

  • General examination
  • Abdominal examination
  • Costovertebral angle tenderness

Differential Diagnosis

Notes

Physical examination

ComponentWhat you are looking for
General examinationVital signs — fever, tachycardia, hypotension point to sepsis; distress, restlessness
Abdominal examinationPeritonism or guarding (surgical abdomen), masses, a pulsatile mass (aneurysm), palpable bladder
Costovertebral angle (CVA) tendernessTenderness at the angle between the 12th rib and the vertebral column — localises the problem to the kidney
Reading this patient's history
FindingWhat it tells you
Sudden onset, severity 10/10Classic for acute ureteric obstruction by a stone
Radiates to the groinLoin-to-groin radiation → ureteric stone
No aggravating / relieving factors; not related to movementArgues against musculoskeletal / radicular pain, which changes with movement
No urinary symptomsDoes not rule out a stone
No GI symptomsBowel causes (appendicitis, obstruction, diverticulitis) less likely
No feverNo clinical sign of infection — uncomplicated colic (for now)
Left flank tendernessSupports a renal / ureteric source

M I M I C S

  • 40-year-old, sudden right flank pain radiating to the lower abdomen, CVA tenderness → right ureteric stone. 435 ×4
Notes

Differential Diagnosis

Flank pain is not always a stone. The lecture's list, grouped by system — the ones in red are time-critical and must be actively excluded.

CAN'T-MISS MIMICS — PRACTICAL TRIGGERS
Older patient with a "first ever" renal colic → think leaking abdominal aortic aneurysm (feel for a pulsatile mass, check BP).
Woman of reproductive age → pregnancy test to exclude ectopic pregnancy; consider ovarian torsion.
Young male with groin pain → always examine the testes for torsion.
Upper-abdominal / referred pain with risk factors → ECG for MI; peritonism → perforated ulcer.

W O R K - U P

Case

  • A 24-year-old male presented with left flank pain for 2 days.
  • Pain radiating to groin. No aggravating or relieving factors. Sudden. 10/10.
  • No urinary symptoms
  • Not related to movement
  • No GI symptoms
  • No fever
  • Physical examination revealed left flank tenderness
  • Next?

Investigations

  • CBC
  • Renal profile
  • Urine analysis
  • Imaging (which one)
Notes

Investigations

Laboratory

TestKey resultWhy it matters
CBCWBCRaised WBC = infection → changes management (see Stage 2)
Renal profileCreatinine / ureaRenal impairment is an indication to intervene
Urine analysisHaematuria; pyuria / nitritesHaematuria supports a stone; pyuria/nitrites suggest infection (send culture)

KUB

US

IVU

MRU

Gold Standard

  • CT without contrast
  • Next?
Notes

Imaging — which one?

ModalityWhat it showsStrengthsLimitations
KUB plain X-rayRadio-opaque stones (calcium)Cheap, quick, low dose; good for follow-up of a known radio-opaque stoneMisses radiolucent stones (uric acid, xanthine); bowel gas and bone overlap
USHydronephrosis (dilated, fluid- filled calyces); renal stonesNo radiation — first choice in pregnancy and childrenPoor at seeing ureteric stones; operator dependent
IVU IV urogramContrast excretion → level of obstruction, delayed functionShows anatomy and function togetherIV contrast (allergy, nephrotoxicity), radiation, slow — largely replaced by CT
MRU MR urogramDilated collecting system; stone seen as a filling defectNo ionising radiationStones themselves poorly seen; costly, less available
CT without contrastVirtually all stones: size, site, density; hydronephrosisMost sensitive and specific; detects alternative diagnosesRadiation dose

Gold standard

GOLD STANDARD = NON-CONTRAST CT (CT KUB)
Sees stones that are invisible on KUB (uric acid)
No contrast — contrast is bright and would hide the stone
Gives what the treatment decision needs: site + size

S T A G E 1 M A N A G E M E N T

  • Renal stones — investigation of choice → CT (non-contrast). 441 ×2

Treatment

  • Hydration
  • Analgesia
  • Medical expulsion therapy
  • When do you admit/intervene?
Notes

Treating Uncomplicated Colic

1 Hydration Maintain fluid intake / IV fluids if vomiting.·2 Analgesia NSAIDs are the usual first line (if no contraindication); opioids for breakthrough pain.·3 Medical expulsive therapy α1-blocker (e.g. tamsulosin) relaxes distal ureteric smooth muscle to help the stone pass.
  • 25-year-old, 2 days of left ureteric colic, 4 mm radio-opaque distal ureteric stone → initial management adequate analgesia and hydration. 438 ×6
Source key vs the doctor's pathway: a 6-mm ureteric stone in a woman with flank pain and no complication was keyed "ureteroscopy". The doctor's pathway for uncomplicated colic is hydration, analgesia and medical expulsive therapy, intervening only for the five indications above — so the answer here is conservative. Choose URS when an indication is present (or MET fails).

Indications

  • Infection
  • Renal impairment
  • Persistent nausea and vomiting
  • Persistent pain not responding to oral analgesia
  • Failure of medical therapy
Notes

When do you admit / intervene?

1 Infection Fever, ↑WBC, pyuria with obstruction·2 Renal impairment Raised creatinine; single kidney; bilateral obstruction·3 Nausea & vomiting Persistent — cannot keep oral intake or meds down·4 Pain Persistent despite oral analgesia·5 Failed MET Stone not passing on medical therapy
MEMORY HOOK — "I REALLY NEED PROPER FIXING"
Infection · Renal impairment · Nausea & vomiting · Pain not controlled orally · Failure of medical therapy

S T A G E 2 · U R O L O G I C A L E M E R G E N C Y

Case

  • Same patient presented with fever and increase left flank pain
  • CBC: Elevated WBC
  • Renal profile : Normal
  • CT: Same
  • Next?
Notes

The Obstructed, Infected Kidney

Same patient returns with fever and increasing left flank pain. CBC: WBC elevated. Renal profile: normal. CT: same stone, still obstructing.

DANGER
Infection behind an obstructing stone = pus under pressure. This patient can become septic quickly — antibiotics alone are not enough; the kidney must be decompressed urgently.

Treatment

  • Hydration
  • Analgesia
  • UA and C/S and blood C/S
  • Broad spectrum antibiotics
  • Urine diversion
Notes

Management sequence

1 Hydration IV fluids→2 Analgesia Control pain→3 Cultures UA + urine C/S and blood C/S — before antibiotics→4 Antibiotics Broad-spectrum, IV; narrow once cultures return→5 Urine diversion DJ stent or nephrostomy — urgently

Urine diversion

DJ stentNephrostomy

Why?

Antibiotic levels are low with obstructionSepsis if definitive therapy
Notes

Why divert instead of treating the stone now?

Antibiotics alone fail
Antibiotic levels are low in an obstructed system — the drug cannot be delivered to and excreted into a kidney that is not draining.
Definitive treatment now → sepsis
Fragmenting or manipulating a stone in an infected, obstructed system pushes bacteria into the bloodstream → urosepsis.
RULE OF THUMB
Drain first, treat the stone later. Definitive treatment waits until the infection has cleared (negative urine culture).
  • 55-year-old, fever, chills, flank pain, pyuria, bacteraemia, sepsis, 6-mm obstructing ureteric stone → percutaneous nephrostomy + IV antibiotics. 442 ×2

Case

  • Same patient presented with fever and increase left flank pain
  • CBC: Elevated WBC
  • Renal profile : Normal
  • CT: Same
  • Underwent DJ insertion and 2 weeks later urine culture was negative.
  • Next?
Notes

Urine diversion — DJ stent vs nephrostomy

DJ (double-J) ureteric stentPercutaneous nephrostomy
RouteRetrograde — cystoscopy, up the ureter past the stonePercutaneous — needle and tube through the flank into the renal pelvis (US / fluoroscopy guided)
Where it sitsInternal; proximal curl in the kidney, distal curl in the bladderTube from renal pelvis exits the skin
DrainageInternal, into the bladderExternal, into a bag (output can be measured)
AnaesthesiaUsually general / spinalUsually local
PlusesNo external bag; comfortable once settledDoes not need to pass the stone; useful when retrograde access fails
MinusesStent symptoms (frequency, urgency, haematuria, flank pain on voiding); must be removed / changed laterExternal bag; dislodgement; bleeding

S T A G E 3 M A N A G E M E N T

Indications

  • Infection
  • Renal impairment
  • Persistent nausea and vomiting
  • Persistent pain not responding to oral hydration
  • Failure of medical therapy

Definitive Treatment

Notes

Definitive Stone Treatment

DJ stent inserted; 2 weeks later the urine culture is negative → the infection is cleared and the stone itself can now be treated.

ESWL

  • https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0hKRYVrlfdI
Notes

The four procedures

ProcedureHow it worksApproach
ESWL extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsyShock waves generated outside the body are focused on the stone (located by X-ray / US); fragments then pass in the urineNon-invasive
URS ureteroscopyScope passed via urethra and bladder up the ureter; stone fragmented (laser) and/or removed (basket). A flexible scope reaches stones inside the kidneyEndoscopic, retrograde
PCNL percutaneous nephrolithotomyTract made from the flank directly into the kidney; stone fragmented and extractedPercutaneous — for large renal stones
CystolitholapaxyCystoscope via the urethra; bladder stone crushed / fragmented and washed outEndoscopic, transurethral
Choosing by site and sizeLecture videos — ESWL: youtube.com/watch?v=0hKRYVrlfdI · URS: youtube.com/watch?v=ayCH5cc0y1M

Ureteric thirds are defined relative to the sacroiliac joint: upper (above), middle (over), lower (below, down to the bladder).

TWO NUMBERS TO REMEMBER
Kidney: 2 cm (above → PCNL; below → URS vs ESWL). Upper ureter: 1 cm (above → URS beats ESWL; below → either). Everywhere lower in the ureter, URS wins.

S T O N E C H E M I S T R Y

  • Left renal stone, KUB shows a staghorn (large branched) stone → percutaneous nephrolithotomy. 438 ×5

Bladder stone

  • Cystolitholapaxy

Ureteric stone

  • Mid and lower ureter: Ureteroscopy > ESWL
  • Upper ureter:
    • > 1cm : Ureteroscopy > ESWL
    • <1cm : Ureteroscopy or ESWL
  • 40-year-old, stable, ureteric stone with hydronephrosis, no infection — among nephrectomy, open surgery, antibiotics → ESWL. 442

Renal stone

  • > 2 cm : PCNL
  • < 2 cm : URS vs ESWL

S E L F - T E S T

  • Coronal non-contrast CT (picture) — diagnosis → kidney stone. 439
  • Flank pain to the groin, haematuria, recurrent UTIs, alkaline urine with urease-producing bacteria → struvite stone. 441
  • 1 cm renal pelvis stone on US, not seen on KUB → uric acid. 429
Notes

Mastery Checklist

If you can explain each of these without notes, you own this lecture.

1
Renal colic = sudden, severe flank pain radiating loin → groin, unrelated to movement — unlike radicular pain, which varies with movement.
2
Before calling it colic, exclude the time-critical mimics: leaking AAA, MI, ectopic pregnancy, ovarian torsion, testicular torsion, perforated ulcer.
3
Baseline work-up = CBC, renal profile, urine analysis + imaging.
4
Imaging: non-contrast CT is the gold standard; KUB misses radiolucent stones; US = no radiation (pregnancy, children) and shows hydronephrosis.
5
Uncomplicated colic: hydration, analgesia, medical expulsive therapy.
6
Admit / intervene for infection, renal impairment, persistent N&V, pain uncontrolled by oral analgesia, failed medical therapy.
Fever + obstruction = emergency: cultures (urine + blood) → broad-spectrum antibiotics → urgent 7
diversion by DJ stent or nephrostomy.
8
Never do definitive stone treatment in an infected obstructed kidney: antibiotic levels are low behind the obstruction and manipulation causes sepsis. Wait for a negative culture.
9
Site/size: kidney >2 cm → PCNL, <2 cm → URS vs ESWL; upper ureter >1 cm → URS > ESWL, <1 cm → either; mid/lower ureter → URS > ESWL; bladder → cystolitholapaxy.
Acidic-urine stones: uric acid, cystine, xanthine; alkaline: calcium, struvite. Radiolucent: uric acid and 10
xanthine.
Beyond the slides

Other urology questions asked (previous "Presentation & investigation" lecture)

Added explanationPainless gross haematuria in an adult — especially a smoker over 40 — is urothelial (bladder) cancer until proven otherwise. Work-up = upper tract imaging (CT urography; IVU in older keys) + cystoscopy — CT can miss flat bladder tumours, so a normal CT urogram must be followed by cystoscopy. Urine cytology helps.
  • 60-year-old with painless gross haematuria, urine full of RBCs → urothelial carcinoma. 436
  • 55-year-old heavy smoker with occasional gross painless haematuria → next CT (urography). 438
  • Same patient, no UTI, CT urogram normal → next cystoscopy. 437 ×4
  • Painless macroscopic haematuria — imaging of choice among US, MRI, IVU, isotope → intravenous urography (CT urography replaces it today). 429
Added explanationA solid renal mass in a fit patient without metastases is renal cell carcinoma until proven otherwise → surgery (radical nephrectomy; partial nephrectomy when technically feasible, especially for tumours ≤ 7 cm). RCC is resistant to conventional chemotherapy and radiotherapy.
  • 55-year-old woman, solid 6 cm left renal mass, no metastasis, normal other kidney → radical nephrectomy. 429
Added explanationThe most reliable urine sample is suprapubic aspiration (any growth is significant — it bypasses the urethra); a catheter specimen is next; midstream is the routine one. Sterile pyuria (white cells, negative culture) → think TB, stones, tumour, recent antibiotics.
  • Most reliable urine specimen to diagnose UTI → suprapubic aspiration. 436
  • Routine check: turbid urine, many WBCs, negative culture (sterile pyuria) — among tumour, stricture, retention, trauma → tumour. 434 ×2
Added explanationBlood at the urethral meatus (pelvic fracture, straddle injury) = urethral injury → retrograde (ascending) urethrogram before any catheter; if retention, a suprapubic catheter. Bladder rupture on cystogram: extraperitoneal = flame-shaped contrast confined around the bladder (pelvic fracture) → catheter drainage; intraperitoneal = contrast outlining bowel loops (blow to a full bladder) → surgical repair. Ureteric injury after pelvic surgery → clear fluid from the drain with low urine output (check drain creatinine).
  • 30-year-old after MVA with blood at the urethral meatus → retrograde urethrogram. 429
  • 7-year-old, straddle injury, urethral bleeding, difficulty voiding → ascending urethrogram. 436
  • Woman after MVA, cystogram with contrast confined around the bladder → extraperitoneal bladder injury. 438
  • 2 days after emergency hysterectomy, drain 800 mL/day of clear fluid, urine 700 mL/day → ureteral injury. 436
Added explanationDelayed haematuria 2–3 weeks after renal trauma treated conservatively is classically from a renal artery pseudoaneurysm or AV fistula (clots cause colic) → CT angiography and angio-embolization.
  • 3 weeks after a managed grade 3 renal injury: haematuria and left renal colic → renal artery (pseudo)aneurysm. 436 ×3
